we have constructed a multi-centennial marine master chronology that has a high signal-to-noise ratio, that we have demonstrated the existence of a significant 13C Sucess Effect (SE) in the Irish Sea, and that the 14C reservoir correction (Δ) is not significantly variable on a multi-centennial scale.

(1) The Irish Sea chronology is the first multi-century, absolutely dated, annually resolved, marine master chronology; and (2) The Irish Sea master chronology is comparable in strength to tree-ring chronologies and has no trend in the ΔR, but may have been more variable in the past.

there is a very significant correlation between the δ13C and the ΔR signals in the shells, but that the ΔR signal is not significantly correlated with the δ13C signal in tree rings.

the chronology is a very significant advance in marine dating and provides a robust, annually resolved, absolute timescale for the marine environment, comparable to tree-ring and coral chronologies for the terrestrial and tropical marine environments, respectively.

this study has produced a multi-centennial, annually resolved, absolutely dated, shellbased marine master chronology, which is fully comparable with tree-ring chronologies and which will allow detailed studies to be made of past climate and environmental variability in the Irish Sea, and more generally of the North Atlantic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the Irish Sea provides a very suitable site for the development of a marine master chronology, which is of comparable quality and resolution to those developed for terrestrial systems.
the Irish Sea Arctica master chronology is an important new tool for the reconstruction of past climate change in the North Atlantic, and for the study of the marine carbon cycle.
it has provided a robust, annually resolved, multi-millennial, absolutely dated chronology for the marine environment, which has already provided insights into the dynamics of the marine environment.

the Irish Sea is a very promising location for future research, and the Irish Sea Arctica Chronology provides the basis for a range of future studies of climate variability in the North Atlantic region.
, in the Irish Sea at least, Arctica shells are a reliable source of annually resolved, high-resolution climate proxy data for the past 5 centuries.
